text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- New information about the murder of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme in 1986 will lead to further questioning. A lawyer told Swedish media this week that his former client Lars Tingstrom, the so called Bomb Man, had said he belonged to a group of four involved in the murder. Tingstrom, who died in 1993, allegedly said he had planned the murder from his prison cell to take revenge on a society he hated.
- The liberal opposition party wants to scrap employeers' fees, one of its board members said in a column.

- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, on Thursday opened the way for cutting its key repo rate further when releasing its latest quarterly inflation report. Interest rates fell and the crown strengthened.
- Six thousand people who deliver newspapers were to go on strike on Friday after wage negotiations between the union and employers broke down late on Thursday.

- It is hard to evaluate the truth in new information about the murder of Sweden's Prime Minister Olof Palme in 1986. A lawyer told media this week that his former client Lars Tingstrom, the so called Bomb Man, had said he belonged to a group of four involved in the murder. But Tingstrom only wrote down fragments of his confession and there are no witnessess to confirm what he allegedly told lawyer Pelle Svensson. Tingstrom died in 1993.
- The weak crown will hamper further repo rate cuts. This is the underlying message in Sweden's central bank's latest quarterly inflation report, the paper said.

- A cooperation agreement between unions and employers on how to set Swedish wages is not sufficient, according to Goran Tunhammar, the head of the umbrella employer organisation, SAF. Tunhammar calls for new legislation ahead of wage negotiations in 1998.

- The head of Sweden's state monopoly on retail sales of alcohol, Gabriel Romanus, dismissed worries that the European Union will order the country to abolish the monopoly, called Systembolaget. "Such an insincere, bantering and one-sided statement to the court can hardly be used as a basis," he said about lawyer Michael Elmer's proposal that the EU court ban the monopoly.
- Thomas Franzen, director of the National Debt Office, warns that the Swedish stock market, up by nearly 13 percent since the start of the year, may face a setback.

- Swedish financial markets are expected to be awash in record large amounts of risk capital this year. However, there are few sizeable new share issues on the home market to absorb the money. This presents a golden opportunity for Sweden to privatise state-owned enterprises, according to Bal Sandhu, European strategist with Kleinwort Benson in London.

- The Swedish government was reportedly on the brink last week of announcing a privatisation of public telephone operator Telia. But a difference of opinion between the Industry Ministry and the Communications Ministry caused Prime Minister Goran Persson to withdraw the proposal, newspaper sources said.

- Britain's largest travel group Thomson has reportedly shown interest in acquiring Swedish travel group Fritidsresegruppen, which includes Fritidsresor, Startours, Atlas, Royal Tours and Blue Scandinavia airline.

- Swedish household appliance maker Electrolux has a head start on the Brazilian market, thanks to its ecologically friendly, freon free refrigerator. Brazil will not allow the manufacturing of products containing freons, which damage the atmosphere, after the year 2001.
